one_liner: Header-only C modified-ziggurat normal and exponential samplers; reference code for the McFarland 2016 algorithm, faster than classic ziggurats.
what_it_does: Generates standard normal (normal()) and unit-mean exponential (exponential()) doubles in C, after a one-time normal_setup()/exponential_setup() call. Drawing from its own bundled SFMT-19937 uniform buffer (MT19937.h), it is not a std::normal_distribution-style distribution object and cannot be plugged into another engine. The repo also ships 2015-era Python (pip fast_prng) and MATLAB/Octave bindings, a long-double table generator (create_layers.py) and a profiling harness with Doornik and Marsaglia-Tsang competitors.
how_it_is_fast: McFarland's modified ziggurat (J. Stat. Comput. Simul. 86(7), 2016): 252/253 layers are built entirely under the density, so about 98.8% of draws exit after one 64-bit uniform, one table lookup and one multiply, with no rejection test. The low 8 bits of that same uniform, which the float multiply discards anyway, pick the layer. Draws that miss go to Walker alias sampling over the overhang/tail areas, and precomputed triangle bounds (min_iE/max_iE) accept or reject most overhang points without calling exp(). The uniform source is a pointer into a pre-filled SFMT block buffer, so the fast path is a pointer increment.
when_to_use: Monte Carlo or simulation code in C that needs very large numbers of N(0,1) or Exp(1) doubles from a single thread and can live with a process-global generator.

As a reference to port: the algorithm already powers Apache Commons RNG ZigguratSampler, and the pedrobtz/zurand R package re-derived its tables, so the C here is the canonical starting point for a new port.
When a classic ziggurat (Marsaglia-Tsang, Doornik) is your hot spot and you want the same exactness with a shorter fast path.
x86-64 Linux/macOS builds with SSE2 where you control the compile flags.
when_not_to_use: Multithreaded code: the generator state (sfmt array, iRandS buffer, global Rand pointer) is process-global with no locking or per-thread instances.
Reproducible experiments: mt_init() seeds only from getpid(), time(NULL) and getppid() and ignores repeat calls, and there is no public seed function.
Non-x86 targets or MSVC: MT19937.h uses __m128i/_mm_set_epi64 (MMX __m64) unconditionally and stores 64-bit values in 'signed long', which is 32-bit on Windows; unistd.h is required.
Code that needs other distributions, float output, or a generic C++ engine/distribution interface; Zest or EigenRand fit better there.
The PyPI package: fast_prng 1.1.2 dates from 2015-06-10, before the 2021 correctness fixes, so pip installs the biased sampler.

integration.dependencies: none beyond libm and POSIX unistd.h; bundled SFMT-derived MT19937.h (BSD) is required
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler with SSE2 intrinsics (README builds with gcc -O2 ... -lm; profile_all.py targets gcc-4.8)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with SSE2, POSIX (Linux, macOS); Windows path partially stubbed but not workable as written
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe: single global uniform buffer and Rand pointer shared by normal(), exponential() and the uniform helpers.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same output distribution as a ziggurat normal/exponential sampler, but a C free-function API on a fixed internal SFMT engine, not a replacement for the Doornik/Marsaglia code's engine hooks or for std::normal_distribution

gotchas: Two correctness bugs found by Alex Herbert were fixed only in Aug-Sep 2021 (PR #1: convex-overhang resampling reused X and flattened the bell curve within +/-0.25; PR #2: off-by-one inflection index in both samplers; a follow-up commit fixed '~4% of sampled values in the 1st overhang'). The README says neither showed up in the first six moments, so the 2016 paper's timings ran on pre-fix code.

The headers define non-static symbols (normal_setup, exponential_setup, global 'rand64_t *Rand'), so including them in more than one translation unit causes duplicate-symbol link errors; keep them in one .c file and wrap them.

Rand is a raw cursor into the uniform buffer: if you mix in the helper uniforms (rand_long, wide_uniform) you must follow the README rule to call MT_FLUSH() at least every two increments, or you read past the buffer.
benchmarks/profile.c has '#pragma omp parallel for' around the timing loop; compiled with -fopenmp it races on the global state, so time only single-threaded builds.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over the miloyip/normaldist-benchmark and cauldron ziggurats when you want the McFarland layout (fewer rejection tests, exp() avoided on most overhang draws) as a C reference to port; pick Zest or EigenRand instead when you need a C++ distribution interface, more distributions, thread-local engines or SIMD batch output, and Randompack when you also need fast uniforms across languages.
verified_claims_summary: The only number in the repo is a README sample run: 7.987 ns per standard normal over 1e9 draws with gcc -O2, clock()-timed, CPU not stated and no baseline row; profile_all.py names gcc-4.8 -O2 on an i7-3770K, but its timings.csv is missing. Outside the repo, the paper's snippet reports median runtimes cut to 53% (normal) and 58% (exponential) of other ziggurats on pre-fix code, and an independent C port in pedrobtz/zurand PR #45 (merged 2026-09-27) measured its McFarland method at 1.08-1.25x the speed of its NumPy-table ziggurat on EPYC 7763/9V74, about 1.04-1.10x on Neoverse N2 and 1.02-1.08x on Apple M1.
status_note: Stale: the last code change was the Sept 2021 bug fixes and the 2025-05-21 commit only added an MIT LICENSE; the repo has 2 issues (both closed) and is small enough to vendor, but the 2015 PyPI release predates the fixes.
